title: Maximum Length of Repeated Subarray
description: Brute force to optimized: re-extending from every pair of starting positions versus a single-pass 2D DP table with an extend-or-reset recurrence.

blocks.caption: Build a 2D table where each cell extends a diagonal matching streak

blocks.text: Given two integer arrays nums1 and nums2, find the length of the longest contiguous subarray that appears identically (same values, in the same order) in both arrays.

blocks.title: Analogy: Finding the Longest Shared Stretch Between Two Playlists
blocks.text: Like comparing two music playlists, song by song, and looking for the longest run of consecutive songs that appears identically in both, no matter where in each playlist that run starts. Every time a song from one playlist matches the corresponding song from the other, the current shared streak grows by one; the moment they don't match, that particular streak ends completely and a new one must start elsewhere.

blocks.caption: A match extends the diagonal streak by one; a mismatch resets that cell to 0

blocks.text: Before checking every pair of starting positions and extending forward from scratch, notice this is structurally the same "extend or reset" recurrence seen in Kadane's Algorithm, just applied to a 2D grid of position PAIRS instead of a single array.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Define dp[i][j] as the length of the matching streak ending exactly at nums1[i-1] and nums2[j-1] (using 1-indexed table positions to cleanly represent an empty prefix as 0).

Observation 2: If nums1[i-1] equals nums2[j-1], this position extends whatever streak existed ending at the previous pair of positions, nums1[i-2] and nums2[j-2]: dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1] + 1.

Observation 3: If they don't match, no streak can possibly end here; dp[i][j] = 0, exactly like Kadane's "reset to a fresh streak" when the extending condition fails.

Observation 4: The overall answer is simply the maximum value found anywhere in the entire dp table, since the longest matching subarray could end at any pair of positions.

Recognizing that this recurrence only ever depends on the single diagonal cell before it (never on rows or columns as a whole) is what makes a straightforward, single-pass table fill sufficient.
This is a direct 2D generalization of the Kadane's Algorithm "extend or reset" recurrence, applied along the diagonal of a 2D table indexed by positions in both arrays simultaneously.
For every possible pair of starting positions (one in each array), extend forward while both arrays keep matching, directly.

items: For every possible starting position in nums1, paired with every possible starting position in nums2, extend forward as long as both arrays' elements keep matching.
Track the length of the longest such matching extension found across every pair of starting positions.

items: Every pair of starting positions is tried explicitly, since this brute force does not yet share work between overlapping matches.
The inner while loop extends as long as BOTH array bounds are respected AND the elements match, stopping the moment either condition fails.
best only ever increases, tracking the single longest matching stretch found across every starting pair.

blocks.text: Every possible pair of starting positions is checked directly, extending forward while matching, so the correct maximum is always found.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n * m * min(n, m)) in the worst case, since each of the n*m starting pairs can extend up to min(n, m) positions.
Space: O(1) extra.

Limitation: re-extending from scratch for every pair of starting positions ignores that the matching streak ending at any pair of positions depends only on the streak ending at the single diagonal pair right before it, exactly like Kadane's Algorithm.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force re-extends from scratch for every pair of starting positions. Instead, build a 2D table where dp[i][j] represents the matching streak length ending exactly at nums1[i-1] and nums2[j-1]. Fill it in a single pass: on a match, extend from the diagonal predecessor (dp[i-1][j-1] + 1); on a mismatch, the streak resets to 0. Track the maximum value seen anywhere in the table as the final answer.

Build an (n+1) by (m+1) table, initialized to 0. For each cell (i, j) from 1 to n and 1 to m, if nums1[i-1] equals nums2[j-1], set dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1] + 1 and update the running maximum; otherwise leave dp[i][j] at 0.
Fill a 2D table where each cell extends the diagonal predecessor on a match, or resets to 0 on a mismatch.

blocks.title: Reading the table
blocks.text: Row i, column j hold the matching streak ending at nums1[i-1] and nums2[j-1] (labels show which array value that index corresponds to). The highest value, 3, appears at row i=5, column j=3, built up along the diagonal through (i=3,j=1) -> (i=4,j=2) -> (i=5,j=3), confirming the matching subarray [3,2,1] of length 3.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n * m), a single pass filling every cell of the table exactly once.
Space: O(n * m) for the table (reducible to O(min(n, m)) using a rolling 1D array, since each row only depends on the row directly above it).

dp[i][j] correctly represents the length of the matching streak ending exactly at that pair of positions, because a match there can only ever extend whatever streak existed at the single preceding diagonal pair of positions (one step back in both arrays simultaneously); any mismatch immediately and completely breaks the streak, since a subarray match must be perfectly contiguous in both arrays. Scanning the entire table for its maximum value covers every possible ending position for the true answer.

The rolling-array space optimization (not shown here for clarity) is possible because dp[i][j] only ever reads from row i-1, never from any earlier row.

blocks.text: This problem is the direct 2D generalization of Kadane's "extend or reset" recurrence: instead of tracking one running streak over a single array, a 2D table tracks a streak over every possible pair of positions across two arrays.

items: Re-extending from scratch for every pair of starting positions instead of recognizing the diagonal dependency that allows a single-pass table fill.
Forgetting to track the maximum found across the WHOLE table, rather than assuming the answer must end at the bottom-right corner (it can end at any cell).

Confusing this with the Longest Common SUBSEQUENCE problem, which allows non-contiguous matches and uses a different recurrence (max of dropping either sequence's current element, not just resetting to 0 on a mismatch).

items: Explicitly connect this problem to Kadane's Algorithm's extend-or-reset recurrence, framing the 2D table as simply applying that same idea across position PAIRS instead of single positions, since this connection demonstrates strong pattern transfer.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Longest matching CONTIGUOUS subarray between two arrays" points toward a 2D DP table with an extend-or-reset-to-zero recurrence along the diagonal, distinct from Longest Common Subsequence's non-contiguous matching.

items: How would you reduce the space usage? Since each row of the table only depends on the row directly above it, a rolling 1D array of size (m+1) suffices, reducing space to O(min(n, m)).

How does this differ from Longest Common Subsequence? That problem allows matched elements to be non-contiguous (skipping over unmatched elements in either sequence), using max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1]) as an additional option; this problem requires perfect contiguity, so a mismatch always resets to exactly 0.

Could this be solved with a rolling hash or binary search instead? Yes, binary searching on the answer length combined with rolling-hash-based substring comparison can achieve O((n+m) log(min(n,m))), though the DP approach is simpler to reason about and implement correctly.

A direct 2D generalization of the Kadane's Algorithm / Longest Continuous Increasing Subsequence "extend or reset" recurrence, applied diagonally across a table indexed by two arrays' positions simultaneously.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(n * m * min(n, m)) time, O(1) space.
Optimized (2D DP table): O(n * m) time, O(n * m) space (reducible to O(min(n, m))).

items: Pattern: 2D DP table with an extend-or-reset-to-zero recurrence along the diagonal
Core Idea: dp[i][j] extends the diagonal predecessor by 1 on a match, or resets to 0 on a mismatch, exactly like Kadane's Algorithm applied to position pairs
